title: Source‐Sink Structures Shape Global Drought Propagation
content:
Abstract

The spatial propagation of drought plays a critical role in shaping synchronized global drought occurrences. As hubs (sources and sinks) for drought propagation, the global role of sources and sinks has not been thoroughly assessed. Identifying key propagation hotspots and tracing their global pathways is essential for understanding how droughts evolve over time and space. Here, five paired drought source (location that droughts move from)-sink (region where droughts are more likely to propagate to) systems at the continental scale are identified: western Congo Basin-eastern Congo Basin, Sahel and savanna regions-Sahara Desert, Labrador Peninsula-Great Plains, Amazon Plain-Brazilian Plateau, Tarim Basin and Tianshan Mountain-Central Siberian Plateau, Stanovoy Range, Yangtze River Basin, Middle East. Analyzing water vapor budget between sources and sinks reveals a pattern of drought propagation from sources to sinks, contrasting with water vapor moving in the opposite path. This exacerbates drought severity in drought sinks, a trend likely to intensify under future scenarios with increased radiative forcing. This study identifies a drought source-sink structure, providing a new perspective on large-scale drought spatial propagation. These offer critical insights for drought early warning and mitigation strategies across regions.
